current.description: A structured map connecting medical ethics, spiritual correspondence, and exact supporting passages without using faith as evidence for disputed facts.

metadata.sourceNote: The readable Atlas and machine projections are generated from current.atlas; this record does not duplicate an authored prose document.

atlas.title: Faith and Medical Ethics Atlas
atlas.summary: A structured map of moral and spiritual principles already present across the publication, connected to medical ethics and to the exact article units that support each correspondence.
atlas.evidence_boundary: Spiritual correspondence is ethical context, not evidence that disputed historical, medical, legal, or professional claims are true.
atlas.cross_faith_note: These entries map moral resonance rather than doctrinal equivalence. Multiple traditions can contain recognizable analogues while grounding and interpreting them differently.
atlas.governing_discipline: Tell the truth carefully enough that the other person remains present to answer it. Hold conduct accountable without claiming ownership of the person. Preserve the possibility of correction where correction remains possible.

principles.title: Truthfulness
principles.summary: Truthfulness means saying what the evidence supports, preserving uncertainty, separating observation from inference and recollection from documentation, and correcting the account when contrary evidence appears.
distinctions: truth is not rhetorical victory
observation is not inference
uncertainty should remain visible
cautions: Evidence should never be made to support more than it can, and another person must remain able to answer.

principles.title: Courage
principles.summary: Courage is courage for truth: the willingness to say "I do not know," consult, revise, permit another person to be right about something consequential, and act when institutional comfort favors inaction.
distinctions: courage is not aggression
uncertainty can be stated without abdication
cautions: Courage does not license domination, accusation beyond the record, or needless injury.

principles.title: Humility
principles.summary: Humility is epistemic and relational: institutional authority does not become certainty merely because it possesses the institutional voice.

terms: revision of a record or conclusion

distinctions: authority is not certainty
independent observation differs from inherited assertion
cautions: Humility is not passivity; it can require a definite correction or consultation.

principles.title: Love / Agape / Charity
principles.summary: Love means seeking truth while continuing to desire the good of the other person. It is compatible with confrontation, refusal, boundaries, evidence preservation, and demands for accountability.
distinctions: love is not sentimentality
love does not require affection or reconciliation
truth and accountability remain intact
cautions: Love must never be used to excuse conduct, erase evidence, surrender a factual dispute, or require forgiveness.

principles.title: Mercy
principles.summary: Mercy is restraint from unnecessary injury when correction, accountability, or protection can be achieved without dehumanization.
distinctions: mercy is not excuse
mercy is not concealment
mercy does not suspend evidence
cautions: Mercy does not require declining investigation, accountability, reporting, or protective boundaries.

principles.title: Stewardship
principles.summary: Professional authority over another person is stewardship rather than ownership: entrusted power carries duties because it controls access, records, interpretation, consultation, and institutional pathways.
distinctions: authority is entrusted rather than owned
power is ordered toward the good of the person in care
cautions: Stewardship must not become paternalistic ownership or a reason to override agency without justification.

principles.title: Dignity
principles.summary: Dignity is independent of fluency, mobility, professional status, institutional convenience, or agreement. A failing voice is not an absent mind.
distinctions: communication impairment is not absence of mind
a person is not reducible to a diagnosis, chart entry, allegation, or conflict
cautions: Dignity does not decide disputed facts; it governs how people are represented and treated while facts are examined.

principles.title: Fidelity
principles.summary: Fidelity means remaining answerable to obligations after an easy procedural step fails; referral, documentation, appointment, or title does not automatically complete responsibility.
distinctions: procedure is not fulfillment
referral does not automatically complete continuity
cautions: Fidelity does not require one clinician to do everything; it requires responsible follow-through and appropriate handoff.

principles.title: Nonmaleficence / Restraint
principles.summary: Authority should not increase avoidable danger merely because an ordinary process permits it. Process itself can enter the risk equation.
distinctions: ordinary process can still produce harm
preserving agency can be part of safety
cautions: Avoiding harm does not mean avoiding all intervention; it requires proportionate attention to the harms created by the intervention itself.

principles.title: Beneficence / Care
principles.summary: Care should be evaluated partly by its effect, not merely its intention, including whether communication is usable, safety improves, consultation occurs, continuity is preserved, and agency remains possible.
distinctions: good intention is not the same as good effect
communication can itself be an intervention
cautions: Beneficence cannot be established by benevolent intent alone and must remain bounded by autonomy and nonmaleficence.

principles.title: Justice
principles.summary: Justice includes equal epistemic treatment: neither physician status nor patient status settles a disputed fact, the same evidentiary discipline applies to each account, and disability must not reduce meaningful access to communication.
distinctions: status is not evidence
equal standards do not require pretending unequal evidence is equal
cautions: Justice must not be confused with forced symmetry; differences in evidentiary support should remain visible.

principles.title: Correction / Metanoia
principles.summary: Correction is the possibility that new truth changes conduct: a person can acknowledge error, revise a record, recognize unintended harm, and act differently.
distinctions: correction is not compelled confession
changed understanding can be expressed in professional terms
cautions: Spiritual language must not be used to coerce confession or substitute for professional error-correction standards.

principles.title: Forgiveness
principles.summary: Forgiveness may be a spiritual category, but it is not a requirement or editorial destination and is distinct from factual agreement, restored trust, absence of consequences, reconciliation, or discontinuing an investigation.
distinctions: forgiveness is not factual agreement
forgiveness is not reconciliation
forgiveness is not absence of consequences
cautions: No patient, witness, or author is required to forgive in order to preserve dignity, safety, evidence, or accountability.

principles.title: Hope
principles.summary: Hope is preservation of possibility rather than optimism about another person's behavior: correction, safer re-entry, communication, and a right act can remain possible while the question remains open.
distinctions: hope is not prediction
preserving possibility does not suspend protection
cautions: Hope must not be used to promise another person's change or delay action needed for safety.

principles.title: Witness
principles.summary: Witness has distinct evidentiary and moral meanings: evidentiary witness concerns what was observed; moral witness concerns refusing to let experience disappear through silence or distortion.
distinctions: evidentiary witness and moral witness are not interchangeable
observation and interpretation remain distinct
cautions: Moral concern does not upgrade the evidentiary weight of a source, and sympathy does not decide what happened.

principles.title: Compassion
principles.summary: Compassion means taking another person's suffering seriously without allowing sympathy to substitute for evidence.
distinctions: treatment can change without changing the evidentiary standard
suffering deserves attention even where causation remains disputed
cautions: Compassion changes how a person is treated; it does not lower the standard required to decide disputed facts.

principles.title: Autonomy
principles.summary: Autonomy requires more than noninterference; it includes conditions in which a person can understand, communicate, consent, refuse, correct, and remain represented across temporary impairment.
distinctions: autonomy is not merely being left alone
communication conditions can preserve future agency
cautions: Autonomy does not eliminate proportionate protection, but protection should return authority as fully and quickly as circumstances permit.

principles.title: Service
principles.summary: Professional authority is ordered toward a purpose beyond the status of the officeholder; in medicine that purpose is the welfare of the person receiving care.
distinctions: occupying a role is not the same as fulfilling its purpose
authority is justified by service rather than status
cautions: Service does not require limitless personal responsibility; it requires using entrusted authority for its proper purpose.

principles.title: Prudence / Practical Wisdom
principles.summary: Prudence is deciding what should be done when certainty is incomplete: recognizing limits, choosing proportionate intervention, distinguishing present risk from disputed historical causation, and acting on what can responsibly be changed now.
distinctions: uncertainty is compatible with action
present protection and historical adjudication are different tasks
cautions: Uncertainty must justify neither paralysis nor overreach; intervention should remain proportionate to what is actually known.

principles.title: Patience
principles.summary: Patience is a communication and ethical discipline: impaired speech, a disputed record, or careful quotation can require more time, and refusal to rush can be part of accuracy.
distinctions: slowness can improve fidelity
time can be an accessibility accommodation
cautions: Patience must not become neglect, indefinite delay, or a reason to leave urgent danger unaddressed.

principles.title: Reconciliation
principles.summary: Reconciliation is possible only where truth, safety, accountability, and voluntary participation make it meaningful; principled non-reconciliation remains available.
distinctions: reconciliation is not forgiveness
reconciliation is voluntary
safety and truth precede relational repair
cautions: Reconciliation is not a required endpoint and must not be used to pressure a person to restore unsafe trust.

principles.title: Custody of Another Person's Words
principles.summary: To quote another person is to exercise custody over a fragment of that person's speech. Exactness, provenance, context, and separation of quotation from interpretation protect that custody.
distinctions: exact words should be exact where exactness is claimed
remembered or approximate wording should be disclosed
quotation is distinct from interpretation
cautions: A quotation must not be made to prove what it cannot, and the same care should apply whether it supports or weakens the author's position.

principles.title: Opportunity to Answer
principles.summary: A test remains a test only while an answer can still matter. Giving another person a meaningful opportunity to answer preserves the possibility of correction without predetermining moral identity.
distinctions: opportunity is not exoneration
an answer can matter without controlling the evidence
a person remains a person while conduct is examined
cautions: Opportunity to answer does not suspend evidence preservation, reporting, investigation, accountability, or protective boundaries.
